newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST-Italy October CPI seen falling to 3.2 pct. [CORRECTED 17:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Italy October CPI seen falling to 3.2 pct. [CORRECTED 17:55 GMT]

text.p: Italy is set to see preliminary October consumer price inflation fall to 3.2 percent from an official 3.4 percent in September despite a rise in petrol and some manufacturers' list prices, economists said.
Ten (corrects from nine) Italian cities are set to publish their preliminary inflation data on October 21 and October 22 with the official October figures published in early November.

Economists said the downward trend in inflation was set to continue after it stalled in September, when it held steady from August's 3.4 percent largely due to the one-off price rises in soccer club tickets at the start of the season.
They see October month-on-month inflation rising 0.3 percent after also a 0.3 percent rise in September against a 0.5 percent rise in October 1995 when the annual rate was 5.8 percent.

Economist Pio de Gregorio at NatWest said the monthly increase in inflation will be due to the rise in petrol and petrol product prices, a rise in quarterly rents and seasonal foods, especially fruit and vegetables due to bad weather.
He added that a brake on price rises will come from the revision in telephone tariff prices.

Economist Bruno Rovelli at Bank of America -- who is looking for a 3.2 percent rate in October -- says his forecast is very positive because October is traditionally a month that feels the effects of seasonal factors such as the rise in tariffs.
Lucia Trevisan at brokers Caboto said after the September pause, CPI will fall in October, November and December in comparison with the same months of 1995 when prices were rising.
"Inflation will fall to 3.0 percent or less in November," Trevisan added.

More pessimistic is Paolo Casadio at Credito Italiano, who sees a monthly rise of 0.4 percent in October from September's 0.3 percent increase. This is due to the rise in some manufacturers' list prices and petrol prices, but the trend onwards was positive as he sees 2.9/3.0 percent CPI in November.
Optimistic on the long-term is NatWest's de Gregorio, "Our long-term prospects remain positive thanks to the rise in the lira that has had a positive impact on imported prices of raw materials".
One uncertainty for the long-term will be the rise in labour costs, and the outcome of on-going talks involving metalworkers and engineers will be watched with interest.
The following are the forecasts of analysts.
